header: IN THE ISLAMABAD HIGH COURT, ISLAMABAD.
Order with signature of Judge and that of
02 22.09.2026 Ch. Naeem ul Haq, advocate for the
body: The office objection as to maintainability merits acceptance. The petitioner seeks to challenge an order of the Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue through constitutional jurisdiction, although the very question whether an appellate remedy lies is itself contentious. Even assuming that no appeal is maintainable, that circumstance does not, by itself, oust the statutory jurisdiction relating to a question of law arising from the Tribunal's order. Indeed, the Tribunal's determination that the appeal was not maintainable may itself constitute a question of law requiring examination in the manner prescribed by the relevant statute. The principle enunciated in CIT v. Scindia Steam Navigation Co. Ltd., (1961) 42 ITR 589 (SC), as to questions of law arising out of a Tribunal's order, is relevant in this regard. The judgment relied upon by the petitioner is distinguishable on its own facts and statutory context and cannot be treated as an authority for bypassing the statutory mechanism in every case.

2. There is also substance in the office's objection that the constitutional petition has been invoked to overcome the statutory period of limitation for the prescribed remedy. Constitutional jurisdiction cannot ordinarily be employed as a means to circumvent statutory limitation or to revive a remedy which has become time-barred. Where the grievance, in substance, concerns the legal correctness of the Tribunal's order, the statutory remedy ought ordinarily to be pursued rather than converted into a writ petition. In the absence of any exceptional circumstance, such as patent want or excess of jurisdiction, warranting interference under Article 199 of the Constitution, the objection is therefore sustained and the petition, in its present form, is not maintainable.
